title: Thousands ‘redundant’ but banks can’t staff their branches
full_text:
Banks are at it again, laying off hundreds of jobs despite reporting billions in profits.
Westpac (with a $7.1bn profit expected in 2026) was the latest major lender to pull the trigger, with a pre-Christmas staff clearance to the tune of 250 jobs, in a bid to “actively manage costs and investment”.
That followed the NAB ($9.1bn 2026 profit) announcement this week that it would shed 2500 staff to “simplify its operating model”.
Meanwhile, both CBA ($10.9bn profit) and ANZ ($7.5bn profit) have made recent job cuts.
Customers don’t think too much about human resources in the banking sector – until we actually need them.
Perhaps you call them to ask why a mysterious fee has been subtracted from your account, only to spend hours on hold.
Or you pay a rare visit to the local branch for something you’ve been told can only be done in person, just to discover a dodgy tobacconist where the branch used to be.
Maybe a relative has died and you’re worried they’re still being charged interest but there’s no way to verify without a code sent to their phone which is now switched off in an e-waste bin at a recycling centre.
If only more people worked at the bank – a place charging you the purchase price of your home all over again in interest, plus a tip, to be a customer.
Last week, I needed to pay a builder’s invoice, which was greater than the $25,000 the bank would allow me to access of my own money at any one time. The only way to pay was at a branch, in person.
There were two branches near my office, both open until 4.30pm. I arrived at the first at 4.15pm. Two staff members were blocking the doorway, speaking a different language.
After ignoring me for 30 seconds or so, they went inside and closed the security door.
“Closed?” I called out.
One looked back with disdain and gave the world’s shallowest nod to confirm. “But you’re open until 4.30,” I called back. She walked away. I made the other branch by 4.25pm. Already closed.
The next day at lunchtime I went to my local shopping centre branch where on arrival I was happy to see only two people in a queue. But comfort gave way to suspicion when I saw signs indicating “zero tolerance” for rude behaviour towards staff. Uh-oh, they don’t have those signs at places with good customer service.
I explained to the “concierge” that I needed to make a significant payment. She said this would be fine, but as they were short-staffed, it was a 45-minute wait.
I didn’t have that long.
The next day, I made sure to get to a branch by 3pm. Finally they could help, though I had to ring the builder to confirm account details in the presence of the bank teller. Of course the builder didn’t answer the first time I called. Or the second. The teller began to shrug his shoulders apologetically.
“Oh no,” I said. “This is the fourth time I’ve come to the bank in three days. This needs to happen today.” Thankfully, the builder answered my next call and I could complete the payment, nearly two hours after arriving.
This is the modern banking experience. So how are staff redundant when there’s a glaring shortage of customer service roles? Sigh, if only banks could afford to keep them on.
